questions.q: In the mixed-dataset approach, what does RewardTrainer need to change about its training process to handle a blend of human-labeled and AI-labeled comparisons?
options: It requires a completely different loss function for each label source
Nothing — RewardTrainer doesn't know or care which source a given (prompt, chosen, rejected) row came from, as long as both are formatted the same way
It requires training two entirely separate reward models and averaging their weights
AI-labeled data must be converted into a different data structure before use
questions.explain: The reward model training objective from Chapter 6 is agnostic to the label source; mixed data is simply concatenated and consumed identically.

questions.q: What is the purpose of computing judge_human_agreement in the second pattern described?
options: To set the KL penalty coefficient for PPO

To check the AI judge's agreement rate with independent human labels on the same comparisons, as a way of validating whether the judge can be trusted at scale before training on thousands of its labels
To determine how many PPO rollout steps to run
To decide which base model architecture to use
questions.explain: This is the independent-correlation check from lesson 40 applied to the AI judge itself — a low agreement rate signals the judge isn't ready to be trusted at scale.

questions.q: In the difficulty-based routing pattern, which comparisons get sent to human annotators rather than the AI judge?
options: All comparisons, with the AI judge used only as a backup
Comparisons where the judge reports low confidence or where two independent AI judges disagree, while routine high-volume comparisons go to the AI judge
Only comparisons involving very short responses
Comparisons are assigned randomly with no regard to difficulty or confidence
questions.explain: Routing by difficulty sends the hardest or most disputed cases to human attention, which is the scarcer, more expensive resource, while the AI judge handles the routine majority.

questions.q: How do the three combination patterns in this lesson relate to lesson 40's reward model evaluation diagnostics?
options: They are unrelated; lesson 40's diagnostics only apply to trained reward models, never to judges or combined datasets

All three are variations on the same underlying idea: don't trust a judgment source without checking it against an independent one, extending lesson 40's independent-correlation check to AI judges and combined pipelines
They replace the need for any evaluation diagnostics entirely
Only the mixed-dataset pattern has any connection to lesson 40, the other two do not
questions.explain: Mixing sources, validating judge agreement, and difficulty-based routing are all ways of using one feedback source to catch another's blind spots, directly echoing the independent-correlation principle from lesson 40.

questions.q: What does Chapter 9 shift to as the reward signal, according to this lesson's closing recap?
options: A return to purely human-labeled preference data with no AI involvement
Verifiable correctness on tasks like math and code, rather than a learned preference judgment from either humans or an AI judge
An entirely unsupervised reward signal with no verification of any kind
A combination of only Constitutional AI principles with no new reward signal
questions.explain: The recap states that Chapter 9, RL for Reasoning, moves the reward signal to verifiable correctness, distinct from the learned preference judgments (human or AI) covered throughout Chapters 6 through 8.
